title: Impact of ocean resolution on the North Atlantic bias in the FOCI-OpenIFS climate model
abstract: Abstract Understanding and addressing biases in climate models is essential for reliable climate projections. This study evaluates the mean state of the North Atlantic in three configurations of the FOCI-OpenIFS coupled climate model, varying in horizontal and vertical ocean resolution. Using 20-year hindcast simulations and observational datasets, we assess the impact of resolution on common biases and their potential drivers. Results show that increasing horizontal resolution in the ocean from $$\sim 50~\textrm{km}$$ to $$\sim 8~\textrm{km}$$ improves the pathways of the Gulf Stream extension and North Atlantic Current which reduces persistent surface biases in temperature and salinity. The high-resolution configuration also produces an AMOC in line with observational estimates. However, the model simulates an unrealistically deep mixed layer in the Labrador Sea. Conversely, increasing only the vertical resolution from 46 to 75 levels leads to an unrealistically shallow mixed layer in the Labrador Sea, weaker dense overflows in the Nordic Seas and a poorly simulated AMOC. In fact, the simulation with low horizontal and high vertical resolution in the ocean performs the worst across most analyzed metrics.
problem: Climate models exhibit persistent biases in the North Atlantic, including misplaced currents and flawed deep-water formation, which are linked to insufficient ocean resolution and limit the reliability of climate projections.
method: This study evaluates the impact of varying horizontal and vertical ocean resolution on North Atlantic biases by running the FOCI-OpenIFS coupled climate model in three configurations and comparing simulation results to observational datasets.
task: The task is to evaluate how varying ocean horizontal and vertical resolution in the FOCI-OpenIFS climate model impacts common simulation biases, such as circulation pathways and deep water formation, in the North Atlantic Ocean.
innovation: This paper evaluates how ocean resolution affects North Atlantic biases in the FOCI-OpenIFS climate model, demonstrating that higher horizontal resolution improves circulation and reduces surface biases, while increasing only vertical resolution degrades performance.

The FOCI-OpenIFS model builds on the global coupled climate model Flexible Ocean Climate Infrastructure, FOCI, v1.0 (Matthes et al. 2020) by retaining the same ocean/sea-ice model and coupler but using the OpenIFS 43r3 atmosphere rather than ECHAM6. The OpenIFS atmosphere model is used here as it is more computationally efficient than ECHAM6, especially at higher horizontal resolutions.
The ocean/sea-ice model, NEMO/LIM2 v3.6, is nearly identical to that used in Matthes et al. (2020).
The exchange of momentum, sea-ice properties, heat fluxes, and freshwater fluxes between the oceanic and atmospheric components is managed by the OASIS3-MCT4 coupler (Craig et al. 2017).

This study focuses on biases in the FOCI-OpenIFS coupled climate model, specifically in the North Atlantic Ocean and the larger Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC).

To resolve mesoscale eddy activity in the North Atlantic Ocean, an ocean mesh must typically be finer than 0.25°, but an even finer resolution, e.g. 0.1°, is required along shelf regions (Hallberg 2013). Models with a non-eddying ocean, i.e. where the horizontal resolution is > 0.25°, are notorious for having a poor representation of the Gulf Stream region.

Another persistent bias, low-resolution models often depict a North Atlantic Current (NAC) that is too zonal (Drews et al. 2015; Moreno-Chamarro et al. 2022; Guiavarc’h et al. 2024), leading to an overestimation of the portion of the current that branches into the North Atlantic Subtropical Gyre (STG), while underestimating the fraction that feeds into the Subpolar Gyre (SPG).
